section.title: The Oracle Against Israel
section.sectionRationale: The trap set by the oracles against the nations now snaps shut. The same formula, for three transgressions, even four, turns at last on Israel itself, and the crimes are not distant war atrocities but the everyday injustice, greed, and sacrilege of God's own covenant people, made worse by all the grace He had poured out on them.
section.thesis: Israel's polished religion masks the sale of the poor, the trampling of the needy, and the silencing of God's word; and against people so richly graced, judgment will fall so heavily that not even the strongest can escape.
section.frameNote: Three strokes: the indictment of injustice and sacrilege; the reminder of God's saving grace they despised; and the sentence that leaves no warrior able to flee.

units.label: The charge against Israel
units.note: the poor sold, the needy trampled

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Israel, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they sell the {{tsaddiq|righteous}} for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.
They trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the earth; they push the needy out of their way. A man and his father have relations with the same girl and so profane My holy name.
They lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge. And in the house of their God, they drink wine obtained through fines.

units.label: The grace they despised
units.note: I destroyed the Amorite, I brought you up from Egypt

verses.text: Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them, though his height was like that of the cedars, and he was as strong as the oaks. Yet I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below.
And I brought you up from the land of Egypt and led you forty years in the wilderness, that you might take possession of the land of the Amorite.
I raised up prophets from your sons and {{nazir|Nazirites}} from your young men. Is this not true, O children of Israel?” declares the LORD.
“But you made the Nazirites drink wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy.

units.label: The sentence: no escape
units.note: the swift, the strong, and the brave all fail

verses.text: Behold, I am about to crush you in your place as with a cart full of grain.
Escape will fail the swift, the strong will not prevail by his strength, and the mighty will not save his life.
The archer will not stand his ground, the fleet of foot will not escape, and the horseman will not save his life.
Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day,” declares the LORD.

tsaddiq.gloss: The righteous or innocent person, one in the right. In the courts and markets of Israel, the tsaddiq was being sold for silver, condemned by bribed judges and creditors for the price of a trivial debt. The word exposes that Israel's injustice was not just unkindness but the deliberate crushing of the innocent for profit.

nazir.gloss: A Nazirite, someone specially consecrated to the LORD by a vow that included abstaining from wine, Numbers 6. God raised up Nazirites and prophets as living gifts of His word and holiness to Israel; the people repaid Him by forcing the Nazirites to break their vow and silencing the prophets, spurning the very grace meant to keep them.

basic.context: After circling all the neighboring nations, God now turns on Israel itself. The crimes are not foreign war atrocities but everyday injustice at home: selling poor people into debt slavery, trampling the needy, sexual sin, and abusing worship. Worse, all of this came from people God had rescued from Egypt and blessed with prophets. So the sentence is that no strength, speed, or courage will save them from the coming collapse.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the climax the whole opening was building toward. God applies the same measure to His own people that He applied to the pagans, and then heavier, because they had received so much grace. The message is that religious ceremony cannot cover social injustice, and privilege does not exempt anyone from God's justice.
basic.originalLanguages: The victims are the tsaddiq, the righteous or innocent, sold for silver and even for a pair of sandals. God recalls that He raised up nazir, Nazirites, and prophets as gifts of His holiness and word, only for Israel to corrupt the Nazirites and silence the prophets. The verdict is total: even the mighty will flee naked.
basic.typology: The innocent one sold for silver foreshadows Christ, the truly Righteous One, betrayed for thirty pieces of silver and handed over by His own people. Israel's rejection of the prophets anticipates the rejection of the Prophet greater than them all.
basic.christ: The righteous sold for silver points straight to Jesus, the Righteous One betrayed for silver and trampled by the powerful. Where Israel silenced the prophets, they would finally crucify the Word made flesh. Yet the Judge who condemns injustice is the Savior who bore that judgment so the guilty could go free.
basic.god: God cares fiercely about how the poor and vulnerable are treated; He counts their oppression as sin against His holy name. He remembers the grace He has given and is grieved when it is despised. And His justice cannot be bribed, dodged, or outrun.
basic.crossReferences: James 5 warns the rich who defraud their workers. Matthew 26 records the Righteous One sold for silver. Isaiah 1 shows God rejecting worship that coexists with injustice.
basic.oneStory: This oracle exposes that God's own people stand condemned along with the nations, deepening the need for a rescue only God can provide. The Righteous One sold for silver, foreshadowed here, will be the very One who saves the unrighteous.

context.literary:
The oracle against Israel opens with exactly the formula the seven before it used, 'For three transgressions of Israel, even four, I will not revoke My judgment,' 2:6. Everything about the form says that Israel is one more name on the list. Then the form breaks. Where the earlier oracles spent a verse or two on the crime and a verse or two on the fire, this one has three verses of charge, four of reminder, and four of sentence, and the fire is gone. In its place comes a cart, a crushing, and a field of runners who cannot run.

The middle block is the structural hinge. Verses 9 and 10 each begin with an emphatic pronoun, 'Yet it was I,' 'And I,' so that the whole account of the exodus and the conquest is narrated in God's own voice, and a long list of what He did is set against a short list of what Israel did. Verse 11 turns the list into a question, 'Is this not true?' and verse 12 answers with a 'But you,' the only direct accusation in the block. The sentence, verses 13 to 16, is the reverse image of the rescue: God destroyed the Amorite's strength in verse 9, and now strength will not save Israel in verses 14 to 16. The warrior who could not be beaten, as tall as cedars, is exchanged for the warriors who cannot get away.

The speed of verses 14 to 16 is part of the art. A run of short clauses, each naming a different kind of soldier, the swift, the strong, the mighty, the archer, the runner, the horseman, and each answered with a failure, leaves no one in the picture who might have escaped. The last line, 'on that day,' is the first appearance of the phrase that will become the book's great alarm, the Day of the LORD, which Amos 5:18-20 explains was a day Israel thought would be hers.
context.historical:
The charges are not about foreign policy. They are about the way a prospering economy treated those who could not keep up with it. In the Mosaic law, a poor man's debts could end in service or sale, Exodus 21:2 and Leviticus 25:39-43, but the law was full of safeguards: no interest on loans to the poor, Exodus 22:25, a cloak taken as security returned by sunset, Exodus 22:26-27, and a standing duty to open the hand to the needy, Deuteronomy 15:7-11. Amos describes people for whom those safeguards no longer apply. A person is sold for a debt as small as the price of a pair of sandals, and Amos 8:4-6 shows the commercial mind that did it: dishonest scales, grain sold with the chaff, and a wish for the Sabbath to be over.

The sexual charge of verse 7 has been read as incest, as the sexual use of a household servant by father and son, or as an abuse of dependent women; whichever it is, the law of Leviticus 18:8 and Leviticus 20:11-12 treats such conduct as defilement, and the phrase 'profane My holy name' is the language of Leviticus 18:21 and Leviticus 20:3. Verse 8 adds that garments taken in pledge, which should have been returned at nightfall, were spread out at the altars, and that wine bought with money from fines was drunk in the house of their God. Religion has become the place where the proceeds are enjoyed.

The history Amos recalls is the shared memory of the nation. The Amorites are the people of Sihon and Og, the giants the spies feared, Numbers 13:32-33, and Numbers 21:21-35 and Joshua 24:8 remember their defeat. The forty wilderness years are Israel's school, Deuteronomy 8:2-5. The prophets and Nazirites of verse 11 are the heart of Israel's own heritage, from Moses and Samuel to Samson, Judges 13:5. By the time of Amos, those who spoke for God were told to be quiet, as Amaziah told Amos himself, Amos 7:12-13.
context.canonical:
The oracle is the sharpest statement in the Prophets of a theme that runs through the whole law: that the way a community treats its weakest members is a measure of its knowledge of God. Exodus 22:21-27, Leviticus 19:9-18 and Deuteronomy 24:10-22 are the law in which the charges are rooted, and Isaiah 1:10-17, Isaiah 5:7-8, Micah 6:6-8 and Hosea 12:6-8 give the same verdict in the voices of other prophets. Amos 8:4-6 repeats his own line about silver and sandals, with the added picture of the market that cannot wait for the Sabbath to end.

The rejection of the prophets in verse 12 becomes a standing pattern. Jeremiah 7:25-26 says that God sent His servants the prophets day after day and Israel did not listen; 2 Chronicles 36:15-16 records that they mocked the messengers until there was no remedy. Jesus takes up the pattern when He says that no prophet is accepted in his hometown, Luke 4:24, and again when He laments over Jerusalem, 'who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her,' Matthew 23:37. Stephen's speech applies it to those who killed the ones who foretold 'the Righteous One,' Acts 7:51-52. The phrase 'the Righteous One' is a title the early church gave to Jesus, Acts 3:14, and the man sold in verse 6 for silver stands behind it.

The New Testament also takes up the theme of the poor and the pledge. James 5:1-6 charges rich believers with withholding the wages of their workers and 'condemning and murdering the righteous,' and declares that the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. The same name for God belongs to Amos, and James is writing in plain imitation of the prophet. Finally, Jesus identifies Himself with the vulnerable, saying that whatever is done to the least of His brothers is done to Him, Matthew 25:40, which gives the charges against Israel a weight that goes beyond the law.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Amos wanted Israel to see that the gap between its worship and its life was not a gap at all but a contradiction. The people prized the altar, the feast and the pilgrimage, and they were very likely sincere. Amos shows them what lay under their own altars: garments taken from the poor, wine paid for with unjust fines. He intended the hearers to feel that their religion was being used as a cover and a place of ease for what the law forbade.

He also meant to rebuild their memory. The long recital of verses 9 to 11 is the nation's creed in miniature: the Amorite destroyed, Egypt left, the wilderness crossed, the land given, the prophets and Nazirites raised up. Amos is not telling them anything new. He is calling them back to what they say they already believe and asking what has become of it. The question 'Is this not true?' is not a request for information. It is an invitation to agree with God before the sentence is read.

Finally, he meant to take away the last comfort a self-confident people had: strength. Verses 14 to 16 describe battlefield skills as useless, one after another. A prospering kingdom believed its safety lay in its army and its wealth. Amos intended to show that the real safety was never there, and that no one, however fit or well armed, could outrun the God who had brought them out of Egypt.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records what Israel was doing and what God said He would do about it. It does not set out a program for the economy. It does, however, tell us what God thinks of certain acts: the sale of a person for a trifling debt, the crushing of the poor, the sexual use of the dependent, the keeping of a poor man's cloak overnight, and the use of the proceeds of injustice for worship. Those are described as sins against a holy name, and they are prescribed against elsewhere in the law. The application is therefore firm: God's people are expected to treat the vulnerable with the justice and compassion that He showed in redeeming them.

Care is needed, though, in carrying the oracle forward. It is addressed to a covenant nation under law, and the sentence of exile that follows is peculiar to that setting. The church is not a nation under Mosaic law, and the same sentence is not being passed on any modern state. What does pass across is the pattern: whenever God's people grow comfortable and then use religion to hide cruelty, the same questions are put to them. The New Testament makes this plain when it asks, 'If anyone has material possessions and sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?' 1 John 3:17.

debates.question: What is the sin of verse 7: 'a man and his father have relations with the same girl'?

views.label: Incest within the household
views.case: Leviticus 18:8, 15 and 20:11-12 forbid sexual relations within the extended family, and Amos may be echoing that language when he says the practice profanes God's holy name. On this reading the sin is a violation of family boundaries that the law treated with severity.

views.label: Exploitation of a vulnerable girl
views.case: The Hebrew word for the girl is a general one for a young woman, and many commentators take her as a servant or debtor in the household who could be used by father and son because she had no power to refuse. This fits the passage's concern for the helpless and the economy of debt.

views.label: A cult practice
views.case: A few interpreters have linked the verse with sexual acts at shrines, because verse 8 mentions altars and the house of their god. The text does not say this, and this reading is held more loosely than the other two.

debates.bearing: The text gives no more detail than the charge, and the three readings share a core: a powerful man treats a dependent woman as an instrument. That is what Amos says profanes God's name, and the application does not need the exact detail.

debates.question: How should we read the sale of the righteous for silver and the needy for sandals?

views.label: Debt slavery
views.case: A debtor who could not pay was sold into servitude for a trifling sum, which matches the repeated line in Amos 8:6, 'buy the poor with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.' The point is the smallness of the price: lives are traded for the cost of footwear.

views.label: Corrupt courts
views.case: The word 'righteous' makes some read the passage as a charge about the courts, where the innocent were declared guilty for a bribe. This agrees with Amos 5:12, which speaks of those who 'oppress the righteous by taking bribes' and deprive the poor of justice in the gate.

views.label: A combined practice
views.case: Others hold that the two go together: a righteous person was convicted by a bought judge, fined, and then sold into debt, so that the legal system and the lending economy worked as one machine.

debates.bearing: The readings differ in mechanism, not in substance. In each, the vulnerable are converted into profit, and what the law was supposed to shield them from has become the instrument.

debates.question: What does the cart do in verse 13?

views.label: God crushes Israel as a loaded cart crushes
views.case: The BSB reads 'I am about to crush you in your place as with a cart full of grain.' The cart is the instrument of a heavy, grinding judgment, and the harvest image fits an agricultural audience.

views.label: The cart groans under its load
views.case: The Hebrew verb can also mean to creak or be pressed down, and some translators read the line as 'I will make you groan as a cart groans when it is full of sheaves.' The picture is then of Israel pressed down beneath the weight of what God lays on them.

debates.bearing: Both readings give a picture of overwhelming pressure that no one can resist. The ambiguity should be admitted, but the verses that follow, in which no runner escapes, make the general sense clear.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the poor man, the 'needy,' who is sold 'for a pair of sandals.' The Hebrew for needy, evyon, is one of the standard words for a person who depends on others, and Deuteronomy 15:11 uses it when it commands, 'open your hand to your brother, to the poor and needy in your land.' Sandals, in a world of small transactions, could stand for the least sum imaginable; elsewhere in the Old Testament a sandal is passed over to seal a deal, Ruth 4:7. The ugly point of the phrase is that the person is valued at almost nothing.

Verse 7 begins with a participle for trampling that Amos will use again, 8:4, of those who trample the needy. The verb names the same sort of treatment as a person kept down by the foot. The sexual charge ends with the verb 'profane,' from chalal, which means to treat a holy thing as common. The thing profaned is not a place or a ritual but God's own 'holy name,' qodshi. The same expression is used for child sacrifice in Leviticus 18:21 and for approaching holy things in uncleanness in Leviticus 22:2, so it carries the full weight of law. To mistreat a human being in this way is, according to Amos, to drag God's name through the dirt.

Verse 8 says that garments are spread beside every altar. The cloak taken in pledge is called a chavol in the law, the pledge or security, and the law's insistence that it be returned by sunset gives the reason: 'for I am compassionate,' Exodus 22:27. Amos exposes the contrast between the compassionate God of the law and the people who sleep on the pledge of the poor in His house.

The emphatic 'Yet it was I,' ve-anokhi, in verses 9 and 10 uses the independent pronoun, which is not needed for the verb and is there to stress who acted. The verb for the Amorite's destruction, shamad, is the strongest verb for annihilation in the Old Testament, and Amos uses the same verb in 9:8 when God says He will destroy the sinful kingdom from the face of the earth. The fruit above and the roots below is a merism, naming the two ends to mean everything. What God did to the Amorites, He now says He will do to those who walked on their ground.

Finally, verse 16's 'naked' is a rare, vivid detail: even the bravest will flee leaving their clothing behind, the fighter stripped of his gear. The word is arom, and it carries the image of someone who ran away with nothing. It is the final proof that strength will not help.

typology.type: The righteous sold for silver, Amos 2:6
typology.fulfillment: The price in verse 6 is a pattern, not a prophecy, but the New Testament takes up its words with a pointed echo. Judas asked what the chief priests would give him and they set out thirty pieces of silver, Matthew 26:15, which recalls the wages weighed out in Zechariah 11:12. Stephen calls Jesus 'the Righteous One' whom they betrayed and murdered, Acts 7:52. The correspondence is that the innocent was sold for a small sum by one of His own. The escalation is that the victim of Amos's world could only cry out, while Jesus went to the sale knowing, and used His betrayal to buy back those who had sold others.

typology.type: The exodus and conquest as remembered grace
typology.fulfillment: God reminds Israel that He brought them out of Egypt and through the wilderness, 2:10. The New Testament sees that exodus as a pattern for a greater one. On the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about His 'departure,' Luke 9:31, which in Greek is the word exodos, and Paul says that Christ has rescued us from the domain of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son, Colossians 1:13. The correspondence is deliverance from a power that could not be beaten by the people themselves. The escalation is that the new deliverance is from sin and death. The type falls short because the exodus generation could still forget, while Christ's redeemed are sealed by the Spirit.

Israel commands the prophets, 'Do not prophesy,' 2:12. The pattern continues until the Son. Jesus says that Jerusalem kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, Matthew 23:37, and the parable of the tenants ends with the beloved son killed outside the vineyard, Mark 12:6-8. Hebrews 1:1-2 says that God, who spoke through the prophets, has spoken in these last days through His Son. The correspondence is rejection of the divine word. The escalation is that the messenger is now the Word Himself, John 1:14, and the silencing becomes the cross, in which God turns even that act to redeem.

The law required that a poor man's cloak be returned at sunset, because it was his only covering, Exodus 22:26-27. Amos pictures the cloaks spread out at the altar, and the law's reason, that God is compassionate, shows where the rule came from. At the cross the soldiers divide the garments of Jesus among themselves and cast lots for His tunic, John 19:23-24, so that the one who clothes the naked is Himself stripped. The correspondence is of the vulnerable, deprived of their covering. The escalation is that Christ is stripped so that believers can be clothed with Him, Galatians 3:27 and Revelation 3:18. It is a pattern in the way God deals with the poor, not a code in the text.

study.christ:
The oracle leads to Christ first by contrast of the kind of people God has in view. The poor, the needy and the righteous whom Israel sells are the ones God stands beside, and Jesus comes to stand where they stand. He announces that He has been anointed 'to preach good news to the poor,' Luke 4:18, and in the story of the sheep and the goats He says that what is done to the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner is done to Him, Matthew 25:40. Amos's sentence against those who crush the needy is therefore not only about the needy; it is about the Lord who has joined Himself to them.

It leads to Christ through the pattern of the sold and silenced Righteous One. The word 'righteous' in verse 6 is generic, a person in the right who is wronged, and the passage does not point to a single person. Yet Peter says to the crowd in Jerusalem that they 'rejected the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14, and Stephen says that their fathers killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One and that they have now become 'His betrayers and murderers,' Acts 7:52. A man was sold for silver, Matthew 26:15, and was killed outside the gate, Hebrews 13:12. The line of those whom Israel sold and silenced runs to Him. That is the NT's own reading of the pattern, and it does not require us to say that Amos 2:6 was meant to predict Judas.

It leads to Christ through the revelation of what the law is for. The cloak returned by sunset, Exodus 22:26, was God's compassion in the shape of a rule. The 'righteousness' of Deuteronomy 24:13, credited to the one who returns the pledge, is real but limited. Jesus does what the pledge-holder could not: He gives away His own garment, takes the debt of the one who cannot pay, and cancels it. Paul writes that He canceled 'the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us,' nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The one who was himself sold for silver is the one who frees those who were sold.

And it leads to Christ through the sentence. The rejected warnings of Amos are not the end of God's dealing with Israel. Amos 9:11-15 promises the restoration of David's fallen tent, and the New Testament sees the promise taken up in the Messiah, Acts 15:16-17. The same Jesus who weeps over the city that kills its prophets, Matthew 23:37, is the one who bore the judgment the city deserved. The crushing that Amos threatened falls, in the end, on Him, Isaiah 53:5, so that the guilty may be pardoned.

A caution keeps this honest. Amos 2 is first a charge about the way Israel treated the helpless, and that remains its main force. The links to Christ are drawn by the New Testament's own use of the same words and patterns, and they are not hidden codes in the text. Christ is the one who fulfils the standard Amos applies, who suffers the injustice Amos condemns, and who bears the judgment that Amos announces.
study.god:
The oracle shows a God who takes personal offence at the mistreatment of the weak. The charge is not only that the law was broken but that His 'holy name' was profaned, verse 7. That phrase bears a great deal of weight. It tells us that the LORD has tied His reputation to the way His people treat those who cannot defend themselves. When the poor are trampled, He is slandered. This is a God who is neither neutral on social questions nor indifferent to the means by which a society grows rich.

He is a God who remembers and rehearses His own grace. The 'Yet it was I' of verses 9 and 10 is the voice of someone who has done everything and is now told that none of it counted. The destruction of the Amorites, the exodus, the forty years, the prophets and Nazirites are all gifts, and Israel's failure is therefore not a lack of knowledge but a refusal of what was given. The emotional register of the passage is not only anger but a kind of wounded loyalty, and it shows that God's judgments follow His love, not replace it. Compare Hosea 11:1-4, where the same history is told as a parent's love.

He is a God who keeps the strong accountable. The Amorites were as tall as cedars and as strong as oaks, and He destroyed them root and branch. The warriors of Israel are the same, and the same God dismisses them. The passage insists that human strength is not what holds the world together. This is not only a threat. It is also the comfort of everyone who has no strength, since the God who is unimpressed by the fast and the mighty is the one who hears the cry of the poor, Exodus 22:27.

He is a God who commissions speakers and expects to be heard. He 'raised up' prophets and Nazirites, and He holds Israel responsible for silencing them. A God who sends a word binds Himself to follow it; a people who silence it cannot complain that they were not told.

For worship, the passage asks whether what we bring to God has been bought with what we took from our neighbours. It is a sober question for any congregation that gathers in comfort. And it asks that we remember our own exodus. The God who destroyed what we could not and brought us out is the God to whom we owe our whole life, and our treatment of the weak is a measure of how well we remember it.

crossReferences.note: Amos returns to his own charge with the market in view. The merchants wait for the New Moon and the Sabbath to end so that they can sell, shave the measure and buy the poor 'with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.' The second passage shows the economy behind the first, in which religious days are an obstacle to profit.

The law behind the pledged garments. A cloak taken as security must be returned by sunset because it is the poor man's only covering, and God says that if he cries out, 'I will hear, for I am compassionate.' Amos shows the contrast between that compassion and the use of garments at the altar.

The command to open the hand to the needy, with the warning not to harden the heart and the reminder that the poor will never cease from the land. It is the positive side of the charge: the poor are meant to be met with generosity, and the refusal is called sin.

The Lord rejects sacrifices, new moons and festivals, and asks Israel to learn to do good, to seek justice and to correct the oppressor. It is the same argument as Amos, that religion practised over injustice is worthless to God, in the voice of another eighth century prophet.

The law of the Nazirite vow, which required abstaining from wine and everything from the grapevine. Amos charges that the people made the Nazirites drink, which is to say that they pressed a consecrated person to break his vow and so removed the sign of holiness God had given.

Joshua recites that God destroyed the Amorites before Israel, and sent hornets, and gave them a land they had not laboured for. It is the same history Amos recites, and shows that the memory was part of Israel's creed. The reminder of 2:9 is a quotation of what they already said.

Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, tells Amos to go back to Judah and never prophesy at Bethel again. This is the silencing of 2:12 in a particular case, with the prophet himself as the target. The verse shows that the charge was not only about the past.

Stephen tells the council that their fathers persecuted the prophets and killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One. He applies the pattern of Amos 2:12 to the rejection of Jesus. The line from Amos to Stephen shows how long the pattern ran.

Judas asks what the chief priests will give him to hand Jesus over, and they set out thirty pieces of silver. The sale of an innocent person for a small sum of silver recalls Amos 2:6 and shows what the pattern comes to in the worst case.

James denounces rich people who withhold the wages of their workers and have condemned and murdered the righteous. The cries of the harvesters reach the Lord of Hosts. It is Amos 2:6-8 in apostolic voice, applied to a church where the same temptation appeared.

study.oneStory:
The oracle against Israel is the moment in the Bible's story where the people God redeemed show that redemption alone has not changed them. The exodus was the great rescue of the Old Testament, and the conquest was the gift of a land. Amos 2:9-10 puts both on the table, and then lists what Israel did with them. The question that hangs over the Old Testament from this point onward is whether a people rescued from slavery can live as free people under God, or whether they will become the Egypt they left.

The answer in the history is that they become Egypt. The poor are sold, the weak are trampled, and the prophets are silenced. Within a generation after Amos, the northern kingdom falls to Assyria, 2 Kings 17:7-23, and the writer of Kings says that it happened because they had sinned against the LORD their God who brought them up out of Egypt, 2 Kings 17:7. Judah follows. The pattern of verses 6 to 8 is not a minor footnote to this history but one of its causes.

But the story does not stop at judgment. The prophets who inherit Amos keep returning to the same two promises. First, God will raise up a righteous ruler who will judge the poor with justice, Isaiah 11:1-5, and who will deliver the needy when he cries, Psalm 72:12-14. Second, God will write His law on His people's hearts so that they keep it from within, Jeremiah 31:31-34, and Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises a new heart and a new spirit. The failure of the people at the level of the heart, which Amos 2 shows with painful clarity, is exactly the thing the new covenant answers.

In Jesus, the Righteous One is sold and silenced, and in that death the debt of the people who did the selling is paid. The church that is born from His resurrection is called to be a community of those who share, Acts 4:32-35, where no one among them is needy. The theme continues in James, who writes to churches that were tempted by the same favouritism, and in Paul's collection for the poor of Jerusalem.

The new creation completes it. The poor are no longer trampled, for 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4. The righteous are not sold but reign, Revelation 22:5. And the God who brought His people out of Egypt and into a land will bring them out of every bondage into a city where there is no more night and no more curse, Revelation 22:3-5.

quiz.q: Why is the oracle against Israel the climax of the opening chapters?

options.text: God applies the same formula used on the nations to His own people, and heavier, because of the grace they despised.
options.note: Israel is the true target; privilege increases accountability.

options.text: It is the longest oracle in the section.
options.note: Its length signals the emphasis, but the point is that God's own people are condemned too.

options.text: It is the only oracle that mentions specific sins.
options.note: Every oracle names sins; Israel's are simply detailed at length.

options.text: It shows God finally taking Israel's side against the nations.
options.note: The opposite: Israel is folded into the same judgment as the nations.

quiz.q: What does selling the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals reveal?

options.text: The innocent poor were sold into debt slavery for trivial sums by a corrupt, greedy society.
options.note: Human lives were traded for the price of a small debt.

options.text: Israel had a thriving sandal and silver trade.
options.note: It describes exploitation of the poor, not commerce.

options.text: The courts and creditors preyed on the vulnerable for profit.
options.note: Right about the exploitation; the sting is that a whole person was sold for a trivial debt.

options.text: People simply could not afford basic goods.
options.note: The charge is active oppression, not mere poverty.

quiz.q: How had Israel treated the grace God gave them?

options.text: They corrupted the Nazirites and silenced the prophets, spurning the gifts of God's holiness and word.
options.note: They repaid grace with contempt for the very means of grace.

options.text: They were simply ungrateful and forgetful.
options.note: True, but the text names active corruption of Nazirites and prophets.

options.text: They kept the ceremonies but neglected the poor a little.
options.note: The charge is far graver: crushing the poor and muzzling God's messengers.

options.text: They honored the prophets and obeyed the law.
options.note: They did the reverse, commanding the prophets not to prophesy.

quiz.q: What does the sixfold picture of collapse in verses 14-16 teach?

options.text: No human strength, speed, or courage can save anyone from God's judgment.
options.note: Every human resource fails; the sentence is inescapable.

options.text: Israel's army needed better training.
options.note: The point is the futility of all human strength before God, not military reform.

options.text: Even the best soldiers will be overwhelmed on that day.
options.note: Right, and the deeper point is that no human resource whatever can avert God's judgment.

options.text: Only cowards will flee, while the brave will stand.
options.note: Even the bravest will flee naked; courage is no exception.

quiz.q: How does the righteous sold for silver point to Christ?

options.text: Jesus, the Righteous One, was betrayed for silver and crushed by the very judgment Amos describes, so the guilty could go free.
options.note: The innocent victim bears the inescapable sentence in our place.

options.text: It reminds us that betrayal is a common human sin.
options.note: True generally, but Scripture ties this specifically to Christ sold for silver.

options.text: Jesus was also rejected by His own people, like the prophets here.
options.note: Right about the rejection; the fuller point is the Righteous One sold for silver bearing judgment.

options.text: It has no connection to Jesus at all.
options.note: The New Testament draws the line straight from this image to Christ.

questions: God counts the exploitation of the poor as sin against His holy name. Where might your comfort or convenience rest on someone else being treated unjustly?
Israel kept up busy worship while trampling the needy. How honest are you about the gap between your religious life and your treatment of people?
They silenced the prophets and corrupted the Nazirites, spurning the means of grace. Are there ways God speaks that you quietly try to mute in your own life?
No strength, speed, or courage could avert the judgment. What are you tempted to rely on to save yourself instead of the mercy of God?
The Righteous One was sold for silver to save the unrighteous. How does it move you that the Judge of Amos 2 became the victim who bore your sentence?

translationNotes.note: For a pair of sandals may indicate either a trivial debt or a corrupt legal transaction sealed by the exchange of a sandal; either way, a human life is traded for almost nothing.
The same girl renders a phrase whose exact reference is debated, a cult prostitute, a servant girl, or a betrothed woman; the point is sexual sin that profanes God's holy name.

Garments taken in pledge alludes to Exodus 22 and Deuteronomy 24, which required a poor man's cloak to be returned by nightfall; keeping it to lounge on at the altar compounds injustice with sacrilege.
